B 31/8; incomplete, consisting of a single folio fragment bundled together with other works in A 49/18. A treatise on Vajrayoginī, both title and author unknown. The opening sections bear some resemblance to Tōh. 1565 (*Yogānusāriṇī nāma vajrayoginīṭīkā by *Dārikapāda).

In the introduction—which is not devoid of a certain poetic merit—the author mentions Emperor Indrabhūti and his *Ḍākinīrahasya*, as well as the unnamed work of his own master concerning the *Svādhiṣṭhāna*. Regarding this, he states that he composed a commentary titled *Svādhiṣṭhānavyākhyā*, which likely still survives in China and contains the author’s name, *Kuṭali*.

The quotation from his master’s work corresponds to a line in Tōh. 2275, where it is attributed to Saraha. Following a lengthy introduction, he teaches *sādhana*, *mantroddharaṇa*, *japa*, *bali*, *tilaka*, *udvartana*, *añjana*, and finally *caryā*. The testimony breaks off at this point; likely not much more remains.

The work must have been popular, since three fragments are found in Nepal, one of which (here labeled A) is almost complete. Ms. B also contains a one-folio fragment of an essay on Mahāmudrā; it is uncertain whether this was part of the same work.

Indeed, in this great desert of saṃsāra—accumulated by the manifold proliferation of the five destinies at the midday heat of the summer of ignorance—there are those whose mental states are gripped by the age of Kali, who lack anyone to tell them the supreme secret king of discourses concerning the means for crossing over, and who, failing to obtain the water of the tree of merit from their good deeds—the provisions of charity and other virtues and the city of confidence in meditative concentration—are carried away by the thieves of sense objects, fallen under the power of the afflictions, and subject to the possession of the great planet of perversion.
Not knowing the path to liberation, they wander again and again in that very same place, deceived by the demon of their longing for the pleasures of existence.

[... [3] Those who, failing to obtain the provisions for the journey consisting of merit such as generosity, the city of confidence that is meditative concentration, and the water for the tree of well-performed deeds; who, having been robbed of even a fragment of virtue by the thieves of perversity, are under the sway of possession by the great demons of perversion; who, not knowing the path to liberation, wander again and again in that very same place, deceived by the piśāca-demon of craving for the face of existence.

Now, regarding this: from the great desert of saṃsāra—comprised of the conceptual elaborations of the six classes of beings who dwell like midday suns in the summer of ignorance and so forth—there is the discourse of the King of Secrets, the supreme method for liberation, which is free from [ordinary] speech; it is for those whose minds are attached to this degenerate age, and who have not yet traversed the path of merit such as generosity, nor attained meditative concentration.

Those whose minds are focused on grasping at things as real have fallen [into error], and they shall not attain the fruit of the tree of virtue— those who possess the karmic imprints of virtue stolen away by the enemies of sensory objects, upon whom the great planet of perversion has descended, who do not know the path to nirvāṇa,
and who are repeatedly deceived by the meat of craving for the pleasures of existence that cause them to wander again and again in saṃsāra.

As if desiring to behold the face of their beloved standing afar; as if wishing to hear the words of their lover; as if longing to smell the fragrance of a passionate woman’s hair-vesture; as if wishing to taste the nectar of a dear one’s lip; as if yearning to touch the abode of the god of love; as if desiring to know the conduct of women; as if seeking to find their own proper place; and as if wishing to consume the fuel of the enemy host.

As if wishing to cause the mountain-peaks of the enemy forces to fall, as if wishing to bring an end to suffering, as if wishing to investigate the continuity of birth, and as if wishing to seize the very foundation of the world—thus, like actors impelled by various sentiments and emotions, they were performers of dramatic representations based on external conviction.

As if desiring to behold the face of their beloved stationed afar; as if wishing to hear the words of their lover; as if longing to inhale the fragrance of the hair-scented unguents of their mistress; as if seeking to taste the nectar of their dear one’s lip; as if wishing to fill the abode of the god of love; as if eager to learn the conduct of women; as if searching for their own sanctuary; as if intending to take up fuel for the destruction of the enemy host; as if wishing to cause the mountain-like armies of the foe to fall; and as if desiring to cool the depths of suffering.

Like those desiring to know the continuity of birth, or like those wishing to grasp the support of the world— thus, like actors impelled by various sentiments and moods, they are performers of dramatic representations based on the perceptions of others;

being full of attachment to what is not reality, never attaining even a fraction of happiness, these worldly beings, who follow the cycle of the three realms and lack instruction in reality, encounter only intense suffering.

"Worldly beings, who dwell in great attachment to what is not reality, never obtain even a slight fragment of happiness; lacking the instruction on reality, they remain bound to the three realms of existence and encounter only intense suffering. Those worldly beings who abide in intense attachment to that which is not the truth, and who never obtain even a trace of occasional, mundane happiness, remain within the three realms of existence and enter only into fierce suffering.

He who has taken up birth in concealment, sustained by hundreds of merits and favored by the power of compassion and mercy bestowed upon them; he who is the mountain bearing the earth that is the support of boundless virtues; the instructor of the unsurpassed path to nirvāṇa; the bearer of the great vow to perform benefit for others throughout many eons; the Vajradhara, the most fortunate Blessed One, known as Śrī Cakrasaṃvara, the King Heruka.

Among them is the Lord Śrī Cakrasaṃvara, known as Herukarāja, the Vajradhara who is supremely fortunate; he has taken up a conventional birth sustained by hundreds of merits acquired through the power of one who delights in compassion and so forth; he is a mountain that supports an infinite store of virtues; he is the instructor of the unsurpassed path to Nirvāṇa; and he maintains the great vow of performing benefit for others throughout no small number of aeons.

On that day—by the power of the companion of loving compassion—he fully assumes birth through the *saṃbhogakāya*, which is not held back from the happy realms; he maintains the ground of immeasurable qualities; he reveals the unsurpassed path to *nirvāṇa*; and he possesses the great heroic resolve of compassion for performing the welfare of others throughout immeasurable eons.

Regarding "Grasping"—the Blessed Lord Vajradhara, the glorious Śrīcakrasaṃvara, the King of Herukas, taught the *Ḍākinījālasaṃvara* as the incomparable method, the secret of all yoginīs, which is auspicious through the practice of the left-hand path and follows the tradition of the Yoginī system; for it is exceedingly easy to understand as the very path of yoga, according to the capacity of those with sharp faculties, while instructing on the means for training disciples according to their individual potential. Thus spoke the Teacher.

The Teacher taught the *Ḍākinījālasaṃvara*, the incomparable method that is the secret of all yoginīs—a lineage following the system of the Yoginīs, auspicious through its left-handed conventions—because it is exceedingly easy to understand as the very path of yoga for those with sharp faculties, while indicating the means for training disciples according to their respective capacities.

Desiring to teach the methods for training those individuals who are suitable vessels, [the Buddha] spoke by means of revealing the *Ḍākinīsaṃvaratantra*, which teaches the secrets of all yoginīs—those who have become beautiful through the conduct of the left and follow the manner of the yoginī because it is extremely easy, solely via the path of yoga, by virtue of their sharp faculties.

And therein, so that they might obtain the instruction on what is difficult to attain by means of an easy method, the Blessed One taught that Prajñā, who possesses a form as Vajravārāhī—the reality of the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) of all phenomena—is by her very nature the essence of the Blessed One.

In this regard, so that they might obtain the instruction on what is difficult to attain by means of an easy method, the Blessed One taught that the suchness of the lack of intrinsic nature of all phenomena is Vajravārāhī, who possesses a physical form as the very nature of wisdom.

Regarding the statement, "The instruction on the stage that is easy to attain shall become one that is difficult to attain"—the Blessed One has taught that the nature of wisdom itself is the embodiment of Vajravārāhī, the suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena which lack intrinsic nature.

And her [forms] are seen to be of many kinds, according to the distinctions in the dispositions and the flow of karma of those to be trained (*vineya*). For fear of increasing the bulk of the book, those various types are not described here in detail; however, what is intended is the ritual manual for the practice (*sādhana*) of the Great Goddess alone, who is two-armed and two-faced.

And her [forms] are seen to be of many kinds, according to the differences in the mental dispositions and the flow of karma of those to be trained (*vineya*). For the most part, they are not stated here with all their varieties for fear of excessive length in the text. Although the various inconceivable distinctions of enlightened activity are seen according to the inclinations of those to be trained, they will not be primarily explained here; rather, the *sādhana* of the single Vajra Goddess with two faces and two arms is clearly described.

And this [work] was composed by the feet of Indrabhūti, the supreme king of great kings, who knew the rules for the means of attaining all the principles taught in the extensive tantras, and who had obtained the lineage of the *Yoginīmata* and the means for accomplishing the siddhi of Mahāmudrā. While expounding the secret of the Ḍākinīs—the characteristics of the path realized within himself—he first set forth the means for winning over the world as the cause for the attainment of the Great Purpose (*mahārtha*). He described the sādhana of the Great Goddess, the recitation of her mantra syllables, the ritual of offerings (*bali*), the rites of *tilaka*, *udvarttana*, and collyrium (*añjana*), as well as, in conclusion, the characteristics of the conduct (*caryā*).

And he—His Majesty Indrabhūti, the supreme king of kings, who knew the rules for the means of attaining all the principles taught in the extensive tantras, and who possessed the means for accomplishing the Mahāmudrā-siddhi through the lineage of the Yoginīmata—expounded the *Ḍākinīrahasya*, which characterizes the path he himself had realized; therein, first of all, as the cause for the accomplishment of the Great Purpose (*mahārtha*), he set forth the *Mahādevīsādhana* as the means for winning over the world.

The extraction of the mantra, the rules for its recitation, the ritual of offerings, the forehead mark, the unguent, and the collyrium have been taught; and finally, the characteristics of the conduct [of the practitioner] are described.

Now—by means of the method for attaining, without exception, the reality (*tattva*) taught in many tantras, through the procedure of the method for accomplishing the siddhi of Mahāmudrā, the great king Indrabhūti, by means of the explicit expression of the secret of the ḍākinīs—the defining characteristics of the path as he himself had realized it—first [attained] the Great Purpose.

Since it is the cause for attaining the siddhis, I shall explain the sādhana of Vajrayoginī—the method for subduing wandering beings—as well as the extraction of her mantra, the ritual procedure for recitation, the activities of the wheel-worship, and the characteristics of the subsequent conduct.

To this it is replied: First, the yogin—whose heart is inclined toward the Lady of Yoga (Yogīśvarī), who is skilled in the propitiation of mantra, who acts under the impulse of zeal for the welfare of the world, whose delusion has been dispelled by the grace of the feet of the excellent Guru, who possesses the skill of accomplished effort free from indolence and pride, who is a practitioner of the means for accomplishing the purpose of the threefold samaya, whose mind is one-pointed and joyful, who has abandoned attachment and conceptual construction, whose method consists in the pacification of the latent tendencies of saṃsāra, and whose mind is refined through the cultivation of the two truths—is a wise one.

One who possesses learning, has many gurus, is free from malice, and is bowed to by ḍākinīs; one who is devoted to the rite of worship and possesses the virtues of the Guru, the Jinas, and the Vajra-woman; one who, through various remaining rites, has completely destroyed all aversion and is a discerning knower; one who is worthy of the company of a true guru, has received the command, and is self-restrained—that mantra-practitioner becomes a virtuous person, desired even by the Jinas. He is declared to be endowed with the wealth of consecration and the goal of practice, dwelling in secret with a specialized understanding of the Gurus of the three worlds, and being free from the arising of the fault of instability day by day.

To this, it is said here: First, the yogin—whose heart is directed toward the Mistress of Yoga (Yogeśvarī), who is skilled in the propitiation of mantra, who acts under the impulse of zeal for the welfare of the world, whose delusion and pride have been overcome through the grace of the feet of the excellent Guru, who accomplishes the purpose of the threefold samaya, whose mind is one-pointed and joyful, who has abandoned attachment and conceptual construction, who has pacified the latent tendencies (*vāsanā*) of saṃsāra by means of skillful methods, and whose mind is refined by the practice of the two truths—is a wise one.

Possessed of learning, having many gurus, stainless, and bowing to the *ḍākinīs*; devoted to the rite of worship, bowing to the Guru, the Jinas, and the Vajra-women; through the ritual of various pierced [initiations], he is a knower of the entire procedure for the intended rites; worthy of the company of true gurus, he has received the command and is a self-controlled mantra-practitioner. He becomes beloved by noble beings and the Jinas, and is said to be consecrated, endowed with power and wealth. By the Gurus of the three worlds, he is regarded with special regard as one who dwells in secrecy, free from the arising of the fault of instability, day after day.

In any place desired for practice—such as the peaks of beautiful mountains, mountain caves, the depths of forests, the banks of rivers, their confluences, auspicious shrines, cremation grounds, empty houses, gardens, great monasteries, vast forests, solitary dwellings, or secluded retreats—and having sat comfortably in a fortunate location purified by the *samaya* water and other means, one should perform the consecration (*adhiṣṭhāna*) with the three-syllable mantra. Then, preceded by the taking up of the *samaya*-pill, one should effect the protection of the site, oneself, and the yoga by that very same mantra.

Then, having illuminated the infinite and boundless world-systems of the ten directions with the spreading masses of pale-red rays emerging from the supreme syllable situated in the center of the throbbing red solar disc located in the middle of the heart of Vija, and having drawn in by means of those very returning rays—which take the form of hooks—the immeasurable circle of Gurus, Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Yoginīs pervading the sky before him, one should first worship them with offerings such as water for the feet and so forth, using the individual external offerings.

The second is homage with body, speech, and mind. The third is the confession of misdeeds by oneself and for the world. The fourth is the rejoicing in merit [of] the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, Śrāvakas, and ordinary beings. The fifth is the vow of non-doing from this day forward until enlightenment. Then, out of a desire to rescue the entire multitude of sentient beings who have been brought under the power of the great whirlpool of sufferings such as birth within the vast ocean of existence— which is a dire calamity ablaze with the fires of the three types of suffering— and because they serve as the cause for both accumulations, the cultivation of the four divine abodes (brahmavihāras) is introduced.

In that regard, one should cultivate loving-kindness (*maitrī*), characterized by the generation of supreme affection toward all sentient beings; then compassion (*karuṇā*), characterized by the desire to rescue them from suffering and the causes of suffering; then joy (*muditā*), consisting of enthusiasm and sympathetic delight in the accomplishment of both accumulations for the sake of one’s own great purpose through practice; and finally equanimity (*upekṣā*), whose nature is the avoidance of the eight worldly dharmas.

because equanimity has the nature of being oriented toward emptiness (*śūnyatā*), one thereby brings about that orientation toward emptiness: *oṃ svabhāvaśuddhāḥ sarvadharmāḥ svabhāvaśuddho ’ham* (Oṃ, all phenomena are pure by nature; I am pure by nature). Even for a phenomenon that is pure by nature, because of the absence of investigation into its unity or multiplicity, one should once again resolve upon it as being empty: *oṃ śūnyatājñānasvabhāvātmako ’ham* (Oṃ, I am of the nature of the wisdom of emptiness).

Thus, one should meditate with all one's power upon that mental state which resembles the expanse of the autumnal quarters, stainless due to the cessation of clouds; which is the accumulation of infinite gnosis; which is incomparable; and which is the cause of the sprout of the wish-fulfilling tree of the [ten] kalpas.

having performed this, the knower of yoga should then pray before him for the awakening of the five Buddhas and the ḍākinīs.

For the praise of the fifty ḍākinīs of the Buddhas:
"May all the Tathāgatas consecrate me with the water-pitchers of the pledge-water."

Immediately following the consecration (*abhiṣeka*), the sound of hand-drums (*ḍamaru*) and kettledrums (*ḍiṇḍima*) is heard in the sky. (*jaya*) from the practitioners (*sādhaka*) and their consorts (*sādhakī*), along with shouts of joy such as *hāhā* and *hīhī*, and cries of "Success! Success! (*siddhi siddhi*), are heard; likewise, various musical instruments such as the *muraja*, *paṭaha*, *paṇava*, *tuṇava*, and *vilikā*; the sounds of large drums (*ḍhakka*), small drums (*huḍukkā*), and flutes (*hikkā*); and the sounds of lutes (*vīṇā*), *vallakī*, songs of praise, hymns, and benedictions are heard on all sides.

I shall gratify the five Buddhas and likewise the ḍākinīs,
for the sake of purifying all diseases and for the accumulation of the equipment of generosity.
For the delight of the five Buddhas and likewise of the ḍākinīs,
and for the purification of all ailments, it serves to accumulate the equipment of generosity.
In the space before him is a cool vessel called "lotus," filled with pure substances like moist drops of lunar nectar, and with five blazing hooks consisting of the five nectars (amṛtas).

One should visualize in the space before oneself a white vessel called "lotus," filled with purifying substances like moist moon-melt and the five nectars, and with five blazing hooks; it is the essence of the nectar of consciousness, possessing the luster of the moon,
and is the embodiment of the mantra presided over by the three syllables.
May I ripen that immeasurable, surging ocean of nectar by means of the great power of primordial wisdom.
Having contemplated the nectar of the mind, which possesses the luster of the moon and is the embodiment of the mantra presided over by the three syllables.
He who, through the great power of wisdom, has gathered together the immeasurable, throbbing ocean of nectar.
Above that is the garland of the three-syllable mantra,
and from that, garlands of pure, fragrant rays;
having expanded them and drawn them back, [one pours forth] streams of nectar.

one draws in a stream of nectar-water.
Therein one should cast [the offerings], for they are the essence of great purpose. ||o||

Then, having consecrated oneself with the three-syllable mantra, one should taste the nectar—which is the very nature of the ambrosial wisdom purified from the seeds of the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas, like an elixir that is the sole repository of virtues, shimmering and distinguished by its extraordinary form, color, fragrance, touch, and flavor—while visualizing oneself in the form of the Hero and Mistress of Heroes (Vīravīreśvarī), who is the essence of all Tathāgatas, and consecrating the tongue into the shape of a single-pointed vajra by means of the syllable *HŪṂ*.

Then, [one should visualize] oneself as the purity of the seed-syllables of the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas—possessing an extraordinary form, endowed with infinite qualities, shimmering and radiant, distinguished by uncommon color, fragrance, taste, touch, and flavor—and having empowered oneself with the three-syllable mantra, one should empower the tongue in the shape of a needle-pointed vajra. Thus, while resolving that one’s own self is the form of the Heroine, the Sovereign of Heroes (Vīreśvarī), whose essence is all the Tathāgatas, [one partakes of] the nectar...

Immediately after tasting the nectar, for one whose heart is well-pleased, the practice of recitation is appropriate; for according to the principle that "the mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated," it is preceded by formal undertaking.

Immediately after that, for one whose heart is well-pleased, the practice of recitation (*jāpa*) is appropriate; for according to the principle that "the mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated," [recitation follows]. Now follows the extraction of the mantra for recitation.

One should write three sets of eight [syllables] for those who know the natural order, together with the moon, the sun, the digit, and the vein; having divided the three forearms, they shine forth one by one within each square-hole.

The three octaves of those known as *svarasa* consist of the Moon, the Sun, and the digit of the crescent moon (*śira*). These are written upon the three forearms... [in the first forearm, the five beginning with *uṣman* are to be carried; and the second belongs to that which stands in *ra*.]
The third [syllable] of the fifth is to be carried forward; the third of the fourth is to be carried forward from this [position].
However, in the preceding square, the first [syllable] of the *uṣman* group is to be carried forward; the second [syllable] of that which stands at the end is to be carried forward.
That which is the third of the fifth [set] is the third of the fourth; it is carried from this [place], O you who carry the uncarried.
The third [syllable] is embraced by the third;
that which was previously joined to the first of the preceding group is now joined with the first of the fourth, which stands at the end of the fifth.

But that which is the fifth obscuration is conjoined with the primordial [light] within the fourth, which abides at the end.
Then, in the second square as well, one should likewise write the third of the fifth, and the very same third above the second;
from within that [square], one should write the fourth.

then likewise the fifth, which is the fourth of the third group.
This is complete with five limbs, embraced by the method of Kamalā, and situated at the end.
Then, having first joined together the fifth [vowel] in that same manner, the fourth consonant of the third group,
which is embraced by the one named Kamalā (the letter *u*) and situated at the end of the five-limbed [syllable],
one should write it thus in the third cell of the grid after having performed this arrangement.
That is indeed the third of the fifth [varga], and at the beginning of the third [varga], it is precisely the third of the second varga.
Having first performed that which was previously enjoined, one should likewise write [the mantra] in the third square-hole.
That is the third of the fifth [class] at the beginning, and indeed the third of the second class.
Above that, one should place the third letter of the fifth group (pa), joined with *evai*.
Then, the second letter of the semivowel group (*ya*), followed by the first letter of the second group (*ca*) and then its fourth (*ta*).
Above that, one should likewise place the third letter of the fifth group (*pa*), joined with *evai*.
The second [syllable] is from the group of semivowels (antasthā), then the first of the second [group], and then the fourth.

One should write that which ends with *syāntam* and begins with *vīrakāyutam*; this is the first. Then, having clearly written the three forms of the *ābandha*—designated by the long third vowels (*ī*, *ū*, *ṝ*)—which stand at the end of the sibilants (*ūṣman*), together with the half-moon (*somārdha*) and the sun (*vibhākara*).
If that which ends in *syā* is joined with *ī*, one should write that which precedes the dental [consonant] therein; that is one.
Having clearly inscribed the forms of those [vowels] designated as "svara" with long third [consonants],
and then those [consonants] followed by an *ūṣman*, one should place three [of these] exactly between the half-moon and the sun.
Then one should place two [syllables] in the second [position] and the meaning of the fifth in the third;
having written the preceding [syllables] in two ways, one should extract that which has its vowel removed, which is the form of the "all-creating" limb.
Then one should perform the second pair, which is for the sake of the third [syllable] of the fifth;
having previously written that [syllable] twice with its vowel removed, one should extract it in the form of the "all-maker" (*sarvakṛt*).

The knower of the ritual procedure should extract this mantra: the third [consonant] ending in *ūṣman*, joined with the fourth [vowel], embraced by the fourth [vowel], its body conjoined with the long vowels beginning with *ā*.
The third [consonant] joined with the fourth of the sibilants (ūṣman) is called *āliṅgita*; likewise, the fourth of the sibilants joined with the fourth [consonant] is also so called.
One who knows the ritual procedure should extract this mantra, its body joined with long vowels and so forth.
Thus concludes the procedure for extracting the secret mantra of all ḍākinīs belonging to the Blessed Great Goddess.
Thus concludes the procedure for extracting the secret mantra of all ḍākinīs belonging to the Blessed Great Goddess.

The Lord of Yogins (Yogeśvara), seeking the grace of the aforementioned *Sarvāḍākinī* mantra, should take the lotus-like bone of a noble woman who has died an untimely death and fashion one hundred and eight pills for the purpose of recitation (*japa*). Subsequently, on the eighth day of the bright fortnight, having fed a noble maiden and with her permission, for the sake of attaining the desired fruit, he should at that very time, during the afternoon, suddenly manifest himself as the Great Goddess before him and place the rosary for recitation in front.

One should bathe [the beads] with a stream of liquor mixed with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*). Having bathed them, one should visualize within each individual bead the radiant seed-syllable of Mahādevī situated in the *suṇasi* maṇḍala, emitting an intense mass of pale-red rays. Then, having consecrated them with the pledge-water (*samayavāri*) combined with sandalwood and saffron, and holding them in the left hand, one should perform the pledge-worship (*samayapūjā*) facing west according to one’s means. Visualizing that very same seed-syllable within each bead, one should begin the recitation for one hundred thousand repetitions over the course of seven days.

Having again fed that maiden and properly performed worship of the Tathāgata, one should afterwards place that very garland upon the left ear, fix the desired object in the mind, and sleep according to the yoga of Mahādevī. In the morning, the goddesses announce the signs of success. Having arisen from bed and performed the cleansing of the face and other rites, one should summon six maidens, honor them as is appropriate, and request their command along with a ritual fee (*dakṣiṇā*). This is the consecration of the mantra-garland (*japamālā-pratiṣṭhā*).

Previously, the Lord of Yogins (Jogīśvara), seeking the grace of the mantras of all ḍākinīs, took the lotus-like bone of a noble woman who had died an untimely death and fashioned one hundred and eight pills for the purpose of recitation.

Thereafter, on the eighth day of the bright fortnight, having fed a noble maiden and with her permission, for the sake of accomplishing the desired fruit, one should—at the time of afternoon on that very same lunar day—suddenly manifest oneself as the Great Goddess (Mahādevī) before one’s face and bathe the rosary in front of it with a stream of liquor mixed with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*). Having bathed it, one should visualize each individual bead as the radiant seed-syllable of the Great Goddess situated within a lunar disc, emitting an intense mass of pale-red light.

Then, having sprinkled [the rosary] with water containing sandalwood and saffron according to the ritual pledge (*samaya*), and holding it with the left hand while facing west, one should perform the pledge-offering (*samayapūjā*) according to one's means. Visualizing that very seed-syllable within each bead, one should begin the recitation. After seven days, [one should recite] one hundred thousand times. Then, having fed that same maiden and properly performed worship of the Tathāgata, one should subsequently take hold of that very garland with the left ear, fix the mind in meditative absorption, and sleep in the yoga of the Great Goddess.

In the morning, the goddesses announce the signs of accomplishment (*siddhinimitta*). Having risen from bed and performed the cleansing of the face and other such rites, one should invite the six young maidens (*kumārikā*), worship them according to one's means, and request their permission accompanied by ritual fees (*dakṣiṇā*). This concludes the consecration of the rosary (*japamālā-pratiṣṭhā*).

Then, having consecrated the *mālā*, on that very day and for the duration of that day, preceded by the yoga of the Great Goddess (*mahādevī*), one should recite this mantra incessantly, day and night, while standing, walking, or lying down. Then, having consecrated the *mālā*, on that very day and for the duration of that day, preceded by the yoga of the Great Goddess, one should recite this mantra incessantly, day and night, while standing, walking, or lying down:
"Having fixed the mind upon the path of subtle yoga, having restrained the breath, and having rendered the body motionless..."
When one is able to repeat the hundred and eight desired [mantras], then there is perfect accomplishment.
Having fixed the mind upon the path of yoga, having restrained the breath, and having made the body motionless;
When one is able to repeat one hundred and eight desired recitations, then there is excellent accomplishment.

For this mantra of the Vajra-women brings about, for the fortunate, the emergence of the women dwelling in the three worlds simply by the heart-recitation; the Son of Great Purpose illuminates the sound of the heart.
For this mantra brings about a state of good fortune for the women of the vajra even from mere recitation performed at the heart.
The woman who dwells in the three worlds arises from the heart-lotus, which is empty of great objects through its radiance.

But when a yogin who presides over the circle of the assembly is harassed by the applications of the methods of yoga, he should recollect the mantra that is the heart-essence of the Goddess; then there shall be vomiting from them.

But when the yogin, the leader of the assembly, was harassed by the ritual applications of the methods of yoga, he recollected the mantra that is the heart of the Goddess and her subsidiary hearts; then, there was the vomiting forth of those [practices] upon them.

He who provides food and drink for young women of noble family on the eighth day of the bright fortnight and the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight— that yogi indeed attains his desired goals by means of the Goddess.
Whoever should have sexual intercourse with a maiden of good family on the eighth or the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight;
For that yogi indeed obtains food and drink, and he attains the desired [objects], O Goddess.
Furthermore, having likewise visualized that stainless [syllable] at the junction of the light of vermilion on the forehead and so forth,
one should write this mantra named Aninditā in the center of the *dharmodayā* and the joined wheel.
Furthermore, having spread vermilion upon a stainless vessel or similar surface that is radiant with light,
one should write this mantra known as Anindita in the center of the circle formed by the union of the *dharmodayā*.

Having worshipped the wheel with the four kinds of fruits, the four types of ground, distinguished flowers, and fragrant substances, along with various ritual offerings, they shall attain that supreme state of Akṣobhya.

Having worshipped the wheel with the four kinds of fruits, the four types of ground and distinguished fragrant flowers, and with various ritual services, that supreme and unshakeable state shall come to be. Then, through the power of continuous recitation in this mantra, which is pleasing to the heart of the Goddess, [the goal is attained].
For people who strive for the welfare of the world, dharma becomes effortless, and it brings about the accomplishment of wealth and sensual pleasure.
If one performs the recitation (*jāpa*) continuously in this mantra, which is the heart and sub-heart of the Goddess,
then for people devoted to the welfare of the world, there will be the effortless accomplishment of dharma, wealth, virtue, and desire.

The Lord of Yogins, while propitiating the mantra of the Mahādevī-yoga, should always, on the eighth and fourteenth days of the lunar fortnight, take a single Kulakumārikā who is favorable to the white [phase], and feed her with wine, meat, and other foods and drinks—up to six of them according to his capacity—with due respect. Having fed them, for the sake of accomplishing all desired aims, he should receive auspicious words from them and then undertake whatever task he has in mind. Thus is the procedure for recitation (jāpa) declared.

By the Lord of Yogins (Yogīśvara), while propitiating the mantra of the Mahādevī-yoga, one should always—on the eighth and fourteenth days of the bright fortnight—take from one to six young girls of noble family according to one's capacity, and feed them respectfully with wine, meat, and other foods fit for drinking and eating. Having fed them for the sake of accomplishing all desired aims, one should receive auspicious blessings from them and then undertake whatever task one has in mind. Thus is the procedure for recitation (japa) declared.

Furthermore, for those devoted to the practice of attaining mundane and supramundane accomplishments (*siddhi*), it is impossible to bring satisfaction to both classes of deities without the performance of *bali* offerings.

Furthermore, for those devoted to the accomplishment of mundane and supramundane siddhis, [this practice] brings about the satisfaction of both classes of deities without the necessity of performing bali offerings.
Then, at midnight or resorting to the three junctions of the day (saṃdhyā), one should perform the offering of the sacrificial victim (balidāna),
facing south, with hair loosened and devoid of clothing.
The offering of the sacrificial victim (balidāna) is performed at midnight or by resorting to the three junctions of the day (sandhyā).
Facing south, with hair loosened and devoid of clothing.
With the five kinds of meat and nectars, such as meat, honey, and jambūlika,
and with fragrant foods and drinks served in skull-cups, he whose limbs are well-scented should remain.
With the five meats and nectars, such as meat, honey, jambūlika, and so forth,
along with foods and drinks, and skull-cups containing fragrant substances for the limbs.
Having placed upon oneself the forms of the wrathful deities one above the other, [one should visualize] the fourfold body produced from the four mandalas.
The four mandalas before one are equal to the four elements.
Having visualized the form of Krodha above [himself], he should place it within his own self.
Having assumed the *ālīḍha* posture in a high position, the practitioner of yoga,
having extracted the Heart-mantra of the Goddess, [places it] upon the sun within the lotus of his own heart.
Having assumed the *samālīḍha* posture in a high position, the practitioner of yoga—
Having extracted the Heart of the Goddess into the sun situated within the lotus of one's own heart.
Then, having emanated the three-syllable mantras consisting of that very essence,
and abiding in the state of empowerment, one should summon the two deities.
Then, having emanated the three-syllable mantras, [one should visualize oneself] as being of that very nature.
Abiding in the state of empowerment, one should draw forth the two deities—

the external and the secret— and thereafter, having illuminated with the rays of the Conqueror those born from the eight fields and situated in the ten regions such as the *pīṭhas*, one should attract them.
The external and the secret, in front and behind—the excellent accumulation of the eight fields.
Having illumined with his own rays those situated in the ten locations, beginning with the pīṭhas.
Uttering the mantra, the yogi should perform the *aralli* and other gestures;
thereafter, he should place the *vajrāñjali* at his heart with the *yoginījālamudrā*.
Uttering the mantra, the yogi performs the *aralli* and other mudrās.
Then, having placed the vajra-añjali at the heart, [one should perform] the mudrā of the Yoginī-jāla.
Whirling it again upon the forehead, which is the means for attaining true bliss,
one should fix the gaze on the tip of the nose with a "phetkāra" sound at the crown of the head.
Moving it again upon the forehead as the means for attaining the bliss of the head,
one should fix the gaze on the tip of the nose with the sound of "phetkāra" at the crown of the head.
Then the hero, the accomplisher of all desired aims, [should recite] the fivefold mantra.
For the pacification of all evils and for the attainment of all perfections.
Then the hero, the accomplisher of all desires and aims, should recite the mantra.
For the pacification of all evils and for the attainment of all perfections.

One should repeat the mantra beginning with *oṃ kha kha khāhi khāhī* and so forth. Having thus kept one’s desired objective in mind, while exhaling with the breath (*marut*) situated at the *sa-śibindu*, one should offer the *bali* offering with enthusiasm. Immediately thereafter, having withdrawn the mantras into this heart-syllable of the Goddess who is seated within the solar orb inside the lotus located in the sky of the heart, and having brought the mantras face-to-face, one should perform the yoga of absorption.

One should repeat the mantra beginning with "oṃ kha kha khāhi khāhi" and so forth. Thus, having kept one's desired objective in mind, one should cause the offering (*bali*) to be given with enthusiasm by means of the wind situated within the lunar disc moving transversely. Immediately thereafter: Having struck the *yoga* located within the solar disc inside the lotus situated in the sky of the heart, and having withdrawn the mantras residing in the syllables of the Heart of the Goddess facing this very [disc], [one should proceed].
Having established devotion toward the guru, the qualities of the teacher, and the community,
one who is awakened should wander about with the thought, "This is the Dharma approved by them," so that he may obtain whatever purpose he has intended.
Having established devotion toward the guru, the qualities of the teacher, and the community, one should wander about.
When that [deity] is pleased, he who has awakened to the Dharma shall obtain whatever purpose he has contemplated.
The ritual procedure for the bali offering has been explained.
The *bali* known as *svayambhava*, which was previously accomplished among the *kula*s through the effort of offering flowers, is to be kept secret;
it is then to be mixed with saffron, *bālaśihlaka*, camphor, *elā*, musk, and other such substances.
One should prepare it with all the various fragrant substances, the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), and the five goads (aṅkuśa);
that [substance] should be kneaded by the hand of a young maiden on the tenth lunar day, which is adorned by the moon.
Holding [the vessel] with his left hand, one who desires the glory of the ten thousand-fold [fortune] should recite [the mantra] ten thousand times;
thereafter, he should apply a very subtle tilaka, shaped like a *nandāvarta* and bearing an irreproachable mark.

Due to the constant application of specific adornments and agitation, there arises a distinguished [state] regarding decoration and disturbance; this is the report of a city-disturbance caused by a bad friend and a woman, possessing immeasurable power.
Thus ends the procedure for applying the sectarian mark (tilaka).
Having prepared a mixture of ash with *kanakadala*, *haridrā*, *ketakī*, *reṇḍa*, *kuṣṭha*, *vacā*, earth from a cemetery, *śrīphala*, varieties of *arka*,
and the medicinal substances *amṛta* and *viṣa*, and having diligently performed the recitation (*japa*) at the time of the moon's eclipse;
And then, by means of that bodily ointment, through the attraction of the minds of those who move in both worlds,
one shall become a Yogīśvarī— a goddess of great significance— bestowing all desired objects.
In cremation grounds, empty dwellings, at crossroads, along rivers, on mountains, and in forest thickets,
the sky-clad knower of yoga, having emerged from the mountain of Āmbara, should wander as he pleases by means of that upward-turning [practice].
The body attains nourishment and great vigor, and there is the destruction of suffering caused by the removal of the defects of cold and heat;
this specific method of anointing the limbs is praised here for one who wishes to enter the path of equipment (sambhāramārga).
Thus ends the procedure for the ritual of anointing with unguents.
Then there was collyrium, its appearance filled with joy, beautiful in its power to enchant, and agreeable;
it was a supreme purifier for the eyes and a perfect adornment for the five-arrowed god.

Having prepared secret flowers, joined them with lotus fibers, and dried them on a cool stone slab, one should fashion a slender wick from that material on the tenth lunar day; then, using human fats submerged within a vessel of lotuses...
Right there at dawn, by means of the light of a lamp placed in a crevice that blazes forth while leaning against the western wall,
one should cause the soot— produced from the syllables fixed within the lotus-heart of the Goddess— to fall upon the cremation grounds and other such places.
Having recited one hundred thousand times the mantra of the Añjana-mūrti, for one who abides in the stage of the ripening of the meaning and form of the mantra,
it bestows the accomplishment of all qualities that have entered the range of vision— the cause of fortune that brings about the attainment of desired objects.
Thus ends the procedure for collyrium.
The entire sādhana of the Goddess, her mantra, the method for recitation, the offering of bali, the tilaka, and the application of unguents are to be understood.
And the application of collyrium is of seven kinds according to the prescribed rule.
These unprecedented [teachings] have been proclaimed here in successive order for the sake of practical application;
they are generally intended for those who have emerged from the world and whose conceptualizations are fixed upon external objects.

And by way of remainder, the characteristic of conduct (*caryā*) has been indicated here in this ritual manual (*kalpa*). "Conduct" (*caryā*) is the means for accomplishing the specific welfare of oneself and others, as understood by the wise.
In the Tantra, it is explained as being twofold through the distinction between the outer, inner, and face-to-face [methods].
And that, when applied to external objects, is the singular practice consisting solely of the means for conventional truth.
Desiring to express that state of the mind in which all forms of conceptual construction have been removed, one will speak of external objects as being merely an object of indifference.
Or rather: there is some indescribable person here who, in the midst of the forest of non-duality, displays a moon-like radiance that transcends the power of speech;
and thus, through devotion to the true meaning, this manifestation appears as a mere indication of the direction toward the reality established therein.

Now, for those who are bewildered, [the world] is being scorched by the fire of the multitude of passions and the like, which is fanned into flame by the playful gusts of the wind of ancient and false latent impressions (*vāsanā*).

For those revolving like a jewel in saṃsāra, the mind—which possesses the characteristic of self-awareness—because its nature is manifested through the fivefold service to external objects such as form and because it is unstable, perceives its own specific characteristics;
and by means of the apparatus of the manifold proliferation of subject and object within the nature of form, it takes itself as its support, just as a mirror reflects an image.
And therefore:
Due to the persistence of an unreal mind through the state of continuous succession,
one's own form appears marked by a circle of false appearances.
In a cognition that is devoid of form, the apprehension of an existent form is precisely this subtle delusion; your state is determined by that.
In a mind dependent upon error, there is a great darkness of delusion: neither eternal, nor impermanent, nor both, nor the locus of heavy qualities.
A person who is under the sway of the afflictions of others is not able to cut them off; rather, [the afflictions] spread further and further until they have gained a firm footing.

Thus, for foolish ordinary beings whose minds are perverted by a conviction established through latent impressions—born from causes distressed by the pain of ignorance due to association with false friends—the entire universe here appears as a single object of worship. Therefore, that which produces form and so forth in the three worlds brings about both enjoyment and liberation; it is the world’s conformity [to reality], the state of perfect peace, and the source of joyful, sublime discourse. Even so, one who possesses a mind restrained by the Great Purpose should apply themselves to honoring the removal of its causes; therein, the greatness of the Great Vehicle unfolds.

This very [reality]—uncreated, unmade, nameless, non-artificial, unfailing, infinite, immeasurable, pure from the beginning, formless, beyond syllables, neither eternal nor subject to annihilation, ungraspable, without a grasper, possessing a nature unlike that of the fragmented world, the ultimate knowledge—is [realized] here in this world, which is crowded with the lotus-thicket of the causes and effects of suffering such as birth; by those who possess the retention of a mind purified by compassion and the like, and who hold fast to the seeds of merit cultivated through a succession of many births—the true gurus.

In the ocean of birth, those who are like a helmsman for a ship that crosses over without oars are found wandering by the power of fate; and the fruitfulness of their pacifying and their own skillful actions—[ends] 16.

Then begins this most interesting discussion on Mahāmudrā (from a different work): "Awakening was shown by the Blessed One through the teaching of the two systems of Yoga and Yoginī, by the power of great compassion and skillful means, as independent of long periods of time, under the name of Mahāmudrā."

And here, because of dependence on the authority of the power of one's own resolve (*svādhimokṣabala*) and because of the possibility of encountering a multitude of instructions from the lineage of gurus, yogins dispute regarding Mahāmudrā, which is characterized by the fruit of teaching in accordance with the two systems (*nayadvaya*).
And thus the members of the society who advocate non-dualism say:

The non-dual mind, which realizes that there is no distinction between the grasped and the grasper, nor between cause and effect, is held to be liberation; it is the maṇḍala of the *Śrīsamāja* and other [tantras] that is primordial nature (*prakṛti*).
This indeed is the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā; it is the very essence of all things, and so forth.
Others, however, speak thus:
There is no correct cessation in the case of existence; how could it occur in the case of non-existence?
When both the assumption of an object and its abandonment cease, that [emptiness] arises by itself.
Furthermore:
There is neither the maṇḍala nor those belonging to the maṇḍala, neither the recitation of mantras, nor asceticism, nor fire-offerings, and so forth.
And again:
The seed of the world, called "non-discursive," is blissful and leads to the realization of the Self.
This knowledge is devoid of sense faculties, inconceivable, and without causal continuity.
Furthermore:
The mind, whose essence is emptiness and compassion, is engaged in the practice of generosity and the other perfections.
"It does not bear the mark of conceptual construction that has passed away, nor does it belong to the level of the qualities," and so forth.

This is merely a dispute between two who are equally attached [to their views]; however, for one who correctly examines the teaching (*pravacana*), it brings forth the fault of contradiction. Furthermore, for those who follow the teaching, there is no great likelihood of error regarding the ultimate (*pāramārthika*) phenomena; rather, there is simply a lack of cultivation regarding many [of them].

Indeed, the Blessed One—having taken upon himself the internal commitment of compassionate application for the sake of delivering the immeasurable realm of sentient beings—does not deceive all people under the pretext of teaching the Supreme Vehicle. For this very reason, the Blessed One is the Teacher of the world by virtue of being non-deceptive; whatever he declares regarding the measure of what is to be known, concerning the paths to heaven and liberation as well as external matters, that word must be trusted.
The simultaneous engagement of those belonging to the lineages of resolute faith and liberation.
By that very same resolute conviction, one should take up the path leading to the noble ones.

But how is it that our mental resolve (*manorāja*)— by the power of the authority of our lineage (*gotra-adhikāra*) produced in previous births, or perhaps through association with such people in this great *mantramahā-* [assembly]— is exactly like that?

Therefore, first of all, the homage is spoken here for the purpose of completely pacifying all obstacles to the yoginī and the meditational deity, and for accomplishing the great collection [of merit]. Regarding the words "Māra" and so forth: *vajra* is both the nature of non-conceptual primordial wisdom (*jñāna*) and the union (*yoga*). It is also the entering into the equipoise of method and wisdom. Furthermore, that is the glorious Guhyasamāja...

From the *Subsequent Tantra of the Passionate One*: "The union of method and wisdom is explicitly designated as 'yoga. That which is non-existent is wisdom, and method is the characteristic of existence. Since this [deity] possesses that, she is Vajrayoginī. Alternatively, because the yogi enters into union by means of her, yoga is non-dual gnosis; since that exists in her...

Because she exists by way of her own nature (*svabhāva*), the Yoginī is Vajravārāhī. Alternatively, that which is to be practiced as yoga is the support (*āśraya*), thus "yoga" refers to the lotus; since she possesses this, she is the Yoginī. For the purpose of defining the specific support, "Vajra" is distinguished as before. Furthermore, it is because she is the unsurpassed application for the perfect accomplishment of the welfare of oneself and others, and because of the [accumulations]...

Because she is the union of the two, and because she is the union of non-dual primordial wisdom (*jñāna*), she is Śrīvajrayoginī. If one asks what she is like: emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is the wisdom (*prajñā*) whose nature is the realization that all phenomena are free from conceptual proliferation; compassion (*karuṇā*) is the performance of the welfare of all beings without exception, without a focal point.

The essence of coemergent great bliss is the method; furthermore, that which is the very nature of the non-duality of emptiness and compassion—method and wisdom—is suchness. Moreover, what is it like? The three realms—the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm—are the vajra body, speech, and mind; that which is their very nature is suchness. It is the nature of the inseparability of the three bodies (*kāyas*).

For that reason, how is she? She is "blazing," like the light of the fire at the end of an eon; her radiance is such because its nature is light that dispels the darkness of ignorance. One should understand that "homage is paid to such a Yoginī. Alternatively, it refers to the union of emptiness and compassion, which is the nature of non-conceptual primordial wisdom (*jñāna*).

She is the Vajrayoginī of Passion (*rāgavajrayoginī*); because she is the nature of the inexhaustible union of method and wisdom, her essence is that of the *sahaja-kāya* (innate body). Regarding the phrase "the identity of emptiness and compassion," this very meaning is profound by way of being a repetition based on another referent, and it is the nature of the phenomena of the completely purified mind through its vast and extensive character.

It is the nature of the *nirmāṇakāya*. Because it makes the three realms permanent through the quality of its own uncommon essence for the sake of sentient beings, the very essence of the three realms is the nature of the *saṃbhogakāya*. Because it is free from the obscurations along with their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), it blazes with light like the fire at the end of an eon, as the radiance of the body illuminates the three realms intensely.

It is the nature of the *nirmāṇakāya*. It is said that the nature of these four bodies is also explained as the Blessed Lady, Śrī Vajravārāhī. Alternatively, one should have firm conviction that the lotus at the navel has its face turned upward, while the lotus at the crown of the head faces downward in the form of a three-sided *aiḥ* syllable; this is to be visualized as the essence of wisdom (*prajñā*). The lotus at the heart faces downward.

The *lta ba* (view) and the *kantha-padma* (throat lotus) are circular in shape, having the form of the syllable *baṃ* with its mouth turned upward; they are of the nature of *upāya*. Likewise, it is said in the *Saṃpuṭa-tantra*: "The wheel abiding at the crown is correctly situated in the form of *ai*; know that which abides in the heart and throat to be like the form of *baṃ*. Thus, [it refers to] the lotuses of the navel and the heart.

*Dang*. Through the movement of *caṇḍālī* coming and going within the two lotuses of the crown and the throat, there is the yoga of entering into meditative equipoise through the single taste of great bliss. Such an *āḥ* syllable is the nature of method and wisdom. The syllable *bām* is likewise. "Vajra" is the nature of bodhicitta; because this yoginī possesses that nature, she is [called] Vajra...

Regarding "By the Venerable Yoginī": the essence of blood, which is the nature of Caṇḍālī, is also the nature of the glorious non-duality, and since that very [nature] is also the nature of Vajrayoginī, she is the glorious Vajrayoginī. What is her nature? The meaning of being the embodiment of emptiness and compassion has been explained previously. Furthermore, what is her nature? As for the "elements" (*dhātu*), they refer to the emanation and withdrawal of the three bodies (*kāya*).

This is according to the specific classification of the *Ba'i bye brag*. As for "nature" (*ngo bo nyid*): that which possesses arising is so called. Why? Because by moving upward, it burns the wheels of the heart, throat, and forehead; then, as the syllable *Hāṃ* melts and moves downward, the three wheels are also restored. Thus, it is said in the *Hevajra*: "By the blazing of Caṇḍālī at the navel, likewise..."

Having burned the five *tathāgatas*, the eyes and so forth are also burned. By being burned, [it becomes] like a rabbit's [mark] dripping with *hām*. Furthermore, how is it? Like the blazing light of the fire at the end of an eon—just as the fire of the eon burns the elements and the blazing fire becomes radiant—likewise, through the application of the fierce goddesses (*caṇḍālī*) and so forth, the blazing [fire] arises from the navel of the fierce goddess.

The channels, dharmas, enjoyments, and the wheels of great bliss are incinerated and blaze with their own radiance. This has the following meaning: the Blessed Lady, whose nature is Caṇḍālī in the form of blood, is the glorious Vajrayoginī; moving upward, she pervades the boundaries of the pores with a multitude of immeasurable subtle light rays that definitely arise from blazing.

On that day, as the winds of the central channel ascend through the path of the Middle Way, the wheels of phenomena (*dharmacakra*), enjoyment (*sambhogacakra*), and emanation (*nirmāṇacakra*) are incinerated. These melt into the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*), and their essence, becoming of one taste, descends below. This nourishes the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense bases (*āyatana*), subdues the conceptual imputations regarding the aggregates and so forth, and [unites] method and wisdom.

One should meditate on the nature of the experience of great bliss as abiding at the navel. Alternatively, the verse that serves as an introduction to the meditation that will follow is: "In this regard, first, the accumulation of merit is the worship of Śrī Vajrayoginī; for worship precedes the gathering of merit. The accumulation of wisdom is emptiness."

One meditates on the deity; therefore, [the mandala] is the essence of emptiness and compassion. This is because it is the indivisible nature of the three-cornered source of phenomena (*dharmodaya*), which is the purification of the three realms. As for the meditation on the deity supported by that, its blazing garland of light is like the fire at the end of an eon, possessing a body endowed with the flavors of intense passion and so forth.

The word "RO" (rasa) is a verse possessing four meanings. Following the salutation, after stating the subject matter (*abhidheya*) and so forth by means of the introductory section for the intelligent, the Teacher briefly spoke on the presentation of the *sādhana* together with its oral instructions; this begins with the words "The Guru... and so forth. Therein, the term "*sādhana*" is a brief indication of the subject matter (*abhidheya*). The collection of the root text is stated as follows:

The words "PA'O" (thus), "the Guru," and so forth constitute the purpose of comprehension. The actualization of Vajrayoginī constitutes the purpose of the purpose. The commentary (*ṭīkā*) is explained as having the characteristic of that which explains and that which is to be explained, or by way of its force, it has the characteristic of hearing and causing [others] to hear. The word "explained" (*bshad*) is the summarized meaning. The recitation of the branch-vajras is called "explanation."

"Endowed with. Regarding the *sādhana*: it is the path characterized by the attainment of the great siddhi of the Vajrayoginī mudrā. As for the phrase "I myself shall explain," this indicates a future teaching in order to clarify the external reality (*bāhyatattva*) that has already been perfected. If one asks what kind of method of practice it is, it is the lineage succession of the Vajra Masters, the gurus.

It is called by that name because it is either the instruction (*upadeśa*) arising from that [tantra], or the philosophical system (*siddhānta*), or the object of experience (*gocara*) of that very reality. It is the meaning of the essential nature of the symbolic terminology (*saṃketārtha*) that indicates the lineage of the sublime gurus. Furthermore, what is it like? It is "supreme" (*parama*) because it is the supreme essence of all means for accomplishment (*sādhanopāya*). Of what [means] for accomplishment? Of Vajrayoga.

MA’I’O. The meaning of that has been explained. Now, one might ask: "But do not the tantras such as the Ocean of Samayas of Cakrasaṃvara explain this sādhana extensively by the Blessed One? Therefore, what is the purpose of another sādhana? To this, it is said: "In brief" means that because it condenses the essential meaning, it is concise, possesses the essential meaning, and is summarized.

This is the meaning of "PA. Now, regarding the description of the characteristics of the practitioner, the method of accomplishment, and the sequence [of practice], starting with the words "First," and so forth: having first performed the recitation of the mantras for the protection of the site, oneself, and the yoga, the practitioner—who possesses the nature of the primordial wisdom of the inseparability of emptiness and compassion—purifies themselves through the ritual bath of mantra from the very beginning.

One should perform the purification (*khrus*). Furthermore, how so? The *bla ma* is the Vajra Master (*vajrācārya*). The Buddha is one who has realized the suchness (*tattva*) of all things to be abandoned and all things to be adopted. With a mind endowed with uncommon devotion toward them, [one should purify]. This is because one possessing faith in the Master will attain the accomplishments (*siddhi*). As it is said in the *Vajrārali*: "From the tantras and from the tantras..."

"In order to obtain the supreme siddhis, which are not visible to the eye, one must always please the guru so that the guru may be joyful. Thus it is said; and from other texts as well: "The guru is the Buddha; the guru is the Dharma," and so forth. Furthermore, how so? "Firm" means irreversible; "to grasp" means to take up; and "enlightenment" (bodhi) is the nature of great bliss, which is emptiness and compassion.

The essence is the body, while the mind is the intellect (*manas*). By generating the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*), one will realize the path through bliss. Furthermore, what is that like? Through the empowerments and so forth, the stains of the wisdom of the Body, Speech, and Mind are washed away; this is the meaning of attaining the complete empowerment. This is because one gains mastery over the Unsurpassed Tantra of the Yoginīs of Reality (*tattva-yoginī-tantra*). By means of this, one accomplishes [the goal].

The characteristics of the *pāpa* (sin/confession) have been taught. Furthermore, from another source: "First, the wise one who possesses faith, having become skilled in the mantras of the Yogīśvarī herself, gains mastery over the elaborations that benefit the world. Following at the feet of the supreme Guru—one free from delusion, sloth, and laziness, who accomplishes the purpose of the three samayas—[he is] one whose mind is pure and reaches its limit."

Having utterly abandoned the conceptualization of "attachment," and having skillfully pacified the habitual tendencies of saṃsāra; possessing a mind that has mastered the engagement with the two truths and is serviceable; endowed with intelligence, vast learning, and immeasurable teachers; I bow down to the ḍākinīs who are free from conceptual construction. Through mastery in the rites of offering, I am devoted to the Guru, the Victorious Vajra Goddess; especially [to those] of many rituals.

"PO YI, [one] possessing the knowledge of all instructions and rituals, who has become skilled in relying upon the sublime guru, and who has received the subsequent authorization (anujñā) and whose auxiliary faculties are disciplined"—thus it is said. If one asks what kind of mantra is used to perform the ritual actions that will be explained: *svabhāva* refers to that which is the essence of those things whose nature is luminosity and devoid of substantiality (*niḥsvabhāva*).

Thus it is said: "Sarvadharmāḥ" refers to phenomena (*dharmas*). What are they? In that regard, worldly phenomena consist of the five aggregates (*skandhas*), the twelve sense bases (*āyatanas*), and the eighteen elements (*dhātus*). As for the presentation of the phenomena of the path, they are the four applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthānas*), the four right endeavors (*samyakprahāṇas*), the four bases of miraculous power (*ṛddhipādas*), and the faculties (*indriyas*).

The worldly dharmas are the powers; the supramundane dharmas are the seven limbs of enlightenment and the eightfold noble path; the qualities of a Buddha are the ten powers and the fearlessnesses. Furthermore, how so? Because they perform the function of a charnel ground, places such as cemeteries are "charnel grounds" (*dur khrod*); [therein dwell] those who are headless, those who are bound upside down, and those who lie prostrate.

The sequence of how those who investigate the single *rtze gcig pa* proceed, abide, sleep, and rely [on practice] at places such as charnel grounds, mountain peaks, rock caves, the roots of trees, riverbanks, confluences of two rivers, the abodes of Maheśvara, empty houses, groves, and sites where great disturbances have occurred.

Regarding the "Laso-ka-pa": in a secluded place, upon a soft seat such as a corpse, the yogic play consists of the union of emptiness and compassion. One remains in the vajra posture with the spine straight, the mudrā of meditative concentration directed toward the tip of the nose, speech ceased, and one dwells in the play of single-pointed mind. How so? It is excellent...

Regarding the term "well-consecrated" (*su-pariṣkṛta*): among the four types of abodes, such as the *sthāna*, *upasthāna*, and so forth, they are *Jālandhara*, *Oḍḍiyāna*, *Pūrṇagiri*, and *Kāmarūpa*. In that regard, the first syllable of *Oḍḍiyāna* is accompanied by a half-moon and a bindu; thus, the syllable *Aum* has the meaning of being well-consecrated. By means of this seed-syllable, the abode *Oḍḍiyāna* is symbolized. In that regard—

The purpose of facing toward the west is for the sake of attaining bliss. Why does one face toward the western direction? It is because this *sādhana* originated from the mouth of Vajrayoginī of Oḍḍiyāna, and because it exists there, and because it is appropriate to have faith in it. Why should one sit? Regarding the words "self and others" and so forth, it is because one's own prosperity would be obscured [otherwise].

Having abandoned the two types of clinging accompanied by desire, one attains the siddhi of Mahāmudrā. "The excellence of others" refers, without effort, to activities such as bringing all sentient beings to maturation and liberation. Alternatively, "the excellence of oneself and others" refers to the accumulation of mundane and supramundane qualities. It is for the purpose of making manifest offerings to these.

Regarding the phrase "following that": it is stated so because, following the act of sitting, one must abandon all conceptualizations of body, speech, and mind. Then, having poured into a lotus vessel the three types of *madana*—derived from grapes, dates, and rice—along with the five kinds of nectar (*amṛta*), one performs the consecration (*abhimantrita*) with: *Oṃ Āḥ*.

Having blessed it with the three syllables *HŪṂ ĀḤ HRĪḤ*, one should take that very water as divine water in the left hand and wash all the limbs—the primary limbs, the secondary limbs, the navel, the heart, the throat, and the head—with the mantra-water. Using those very divine substances, one should offer the offering substances as an act of worship.

One should perform the *bsang gtor* (purificatory offering) for the Red Goddess (*Te-me Tog Dmar-po*) and so forth. Regarding the phrase "following that," it means following the *bsang gtor*, one should understand [the placement] on the fingers of the left hand and also on the palm of the hand. Therein, on the middle finger, the little finger, the ring finger, the index finger, the middle finger, and the thumb of the left hand, respectively, are Vārāhī, Yamamathani, and [the others].

Dang, the Bewildering One; Skye-byed-ma, the Procreating One; Sdigs-byed-ma, the Sinful One; and the one whose nature is fierce—red, blue, white, yellow, greenish-yellow, and smoke-colored. Having purified [the elements] with these syllables: *Oṃ Bāṃ Hāṃ Yōṃ Hrīṃ Mōṃ Hrēṃ Hrīṃ Hūṃ Hūṃ Phaṭ Phaṭ*, they are adorned with the mantras of the six yoginīs. Thus, the yoginī...

Because these syllables of the *ḍrūg* (syllable-mantras) are inseparable from the mantra and the deity, one should visualize these very mantras as the six yoginīs (*ṣaḍyoginī*), perform the purification, and carry out the offerings and so forth. This is how it should be understood. By means of the water consecrated by the three syllables, one is thoroughly purified in body, speech, and mind. This is the merit of this very reality (*tattva*).

This concludes the complete accumulation [of the offerings]. However, some, having set aside the sequence of the root text, state the following: "One should visualize the syllables of the mantras of the six yoginīs upon the fingers of the left hand, which have been empowered by the divine water; having made an offering with that divine water, one should perform the purification and scattering (*vighasa*) for the primary and secondary limbs, such as the navel and so forth. Then, with that very same divine water, [one sprinkles] the flowers..."

One should perform the ritual of offering the torma for the sake of those belonging to the northern direction. With that same divine water, one should draw a *dharmodaya* with the left hand in the *srin-lag* (monkey-hand) gesture. In its center, one should meditate on Śrī Vajrayoginī instantaneously. One should then perform the offerings of flowers and so forth, from prostration up to the meditation on equanimity (*upekṣā*). This does not require taking refuge and so forth; it is for individuals of the sharpest faculties.

They say, "Because of this. Therefore, this itself is the collection of merit (*puṇyasaṃbhāra*). Now, for the purpose of accumulating the collection of wisdom (*jñānasaṃbhāra*) following the collection of merit, the meditation on the meaning of emptiness is [described] by the passage beginning with "the three purities" (*trividhaśuddhi*). Regarding that, as for how emptiness is meditated upon here: it is by means of meditating on all phenomena as being without intrinsic entity (*abhāva*), which [purifies] what has been accumulated since beginningless time.

Having first purified the stains arising from the causes of ordinary beings and thereby preceded by the complete relinquishing of the grasping at the aggregates of an ordinary person, one should meditate on the deity through the two stages of generation and completion. In this context, the meditation on emptiness—by way of reasoning—is the absence of intrinsic nature in the single essence of the mind, which is devoid of the subject-object duality of all phenomena; this is emptiness. This...

All external things, such as blue and so forth, and internal things, such as the eye and so forth, are superimpositions. This is because non-sentient entities are not distinct from the mind; since they do not exist, the grasper also does not exist, for it is untenable for a single mind to have a dual nature. If, however, the mind alone were real, that would not be the case, because [the mind] is included within all phenomena, and therefore, regarding that [mind] as well, there is no entity...

This is for the sake of internalizing [the meaning] correctly. Because phenomena lack intrinsic entity (*bhāva*), they are unarisen. By their very nature, they are luminous, being free from the darkness of all conceptual superimpositions (*samāropa*). This is because they have never arisen from the very beginning. That which, having first arisen, subsequently undergoes disintegration—that does not exist. Therefore, phenomena...

Just as with the "illusion of another" and so forth, the mind is likewise empty of an ultimate entity that has never arisen from the very beginning; this is because they are equivalent by way of reasoning. Having thus demonstrated this for the present, one then demonstrates it generally for the past and future as well, thereby teaching the three doors of liberation, such as emptiness and so forth. This...

Regarding the statement, "The three purities shall now be explained": one should recite the three mantras that are completely pure through the three aspects of nature, vajra, and yoga. Among these, by means of the emptiness of intrinsic nature, one is stainless because of being free from existence and non-existence, as well as the superimpositions of subject and object. All the aggregates and so forth, as well as the self, are likewise...

It is so, because it is included within all phenomena (*dharma*). As it is said: "Vajra is emptiness; emptiness is to be expressed as Vajra. Therefore, it is pure through the complete removal of all conceptual signs (*nimitta*) and the clearing away of mental elaborations (*prapañca*). Yoga is the bodhicitta, which is pure through being free from aspiration (*praṇidhāna*). This is because the grasping at a self (*ātman*) is difficult to abandon; for the self itself—

This is because it is said that they "arise from natural purity" and so forth. Through the three mantras, the three doors of liberation—emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*)—are explained. Although [the mind] is completely pure by nature, these [three doors] serve to remove adventitious stains. Following that, preceded by aspiration, through great compassion, one emerges from emptiness.

Regarding the statement that one should meditate on oneself in the form of the deity at this point, the phrase "from that," and so forth, means as follows: immediately following that emptiness, one's own body—the three realms consisting of the three aspects of body, speech, and mind—becomes completely purified. Since the celestial mansion (*vimāna*), the palace of the mandala, is also that very [purification], it is the celestial mansion purified of the three realms. Furthermore, the three realms are also the celestial mansion.

The celestial palace (*vimāna*) is completely pure. Then, one's own body and these three realms are not separate from the celestial palace. Sentient beings are the Victors; I am the Lord of the Mandala (*cakreśvara*). I am not a non-human, nor a land, nor the sense faculties, and so forth. I am not the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) such as form and so on; rather, I am these [beings] arisen from the mandala. Knowing all the various mandalas, I am the uncontrived mandala.

"What kind of mandala, drawn from the *Khor bor nas btags pa*, should be meditated upon? Thus it is explained in the *Kālacakra*. One should have intense conviction that it is a celestial palace (*vimāna*) purified of the three realms; in an instant, without depending on seed-syllables or hand-gestures (*mudrā*), the yogi should always meditate on Śrī Vajrayoginī within the central mandala. To what extent is this so? [The text continues: "..."

Two-armed, holding a curved knife in the right hand and a skull-cup in the left, with hair hanging loose and flowing downward, naked, with two faces and three eyes. "Lang-tso" means one who is twelve years of age, appearing as if enchanting. Adorned with the five mudrās—namely, the wheel, the earrings, the necklace, the bracelets, and the belt. "The five Buddhas" refers to...

The head is adorned with five skulls. "Half-lotus posture" (ardhaparyaṅka) means that the right foot is placed upon the level of the left hip. "Moon" refers to the syllable *roṃ* according to the *Bṛṅga* dialect. Above that is the solar maṇḍala. "Fire" refers to the triangular source of phenomena (*dharmodaya*), which is broad at the top and narrow at the bottom. "Maṇḍala" refers to the maṇḍalas of the moon, sun, and fire.

Regarding "dwelling," the phrase "equal to the *jāba* and *sindūra*" means that the *ādī* flower and the *sindūra* itself are red. She is called "Goddess" (*devī*) because she takes delight in her own excellence (*saṃpatti*). She is said to have "two faces": the right face is that of a sow, and the left face possesses the expression of a wrathful one; thus, she is a "Wrathful Goddess. The purification of these two faces is as follows: "the relative truth," and so forth.

The purity of the two truths consists of the two faces. To express another purity pertaining to the stages: Vajravārāhī is the purity of Vajrasattva or Vairocana. Through the purity of suchness, she is Vajravārāhī. Through the purity of the two truths, there are the two feet and two hands. Without observing the three realms...

The half-vajra posture (*vajraparyaṅka*) represents the purity of [the intent] for the sake of the Teachings. The slight touch of the heels upon the seat represents the purity of attachment to great compassion that never abandons anyone. The six eyes represent the purity of the six superknowledges (*abhijñā*). The faces of the wrathful goddesses represent the thorough abandonment of wrong views. The sow face represents the purity of delusion (*moha*).

The red color is the purification of the activity of empowerment and compassion. The loose locks of hair on the head are the purification of non-dual suchness, which gives rise to the eighty thousand aggregates of Dharma. The vajra garland at the forehead is the purification of the five wisdoms, such as the mirror-like wisdom. The five skull-cups are the purification of the conceptualizations of the five families. [The five] Tathāgatas...
