Through the purity of the [five aggregates], there are the five mudrās, such as the wheel and so forth; through the purity of Vajrasattva, there is the ash; through the purity of the *ālikāli*, there is the garland of fifty human heads; through the purity of existence and non-existence, there is the curved knife (*kartṛkā*); through the purity of the bodhicitta, there is the *khaṭvāṅga*; and through the purity of the flavor of great bliss and compassion, there is the *śam*.

Through the purity of having conquered the four māras, there is a skull-cup filled with blood. To demonstrate the inseparability of the suchness (*tathatā*) of the Tathāgatas and the suchness of all wandering beings without exception, there is a lotus seat, pure because it is unstained by the faults of dwelling in saṃsāra. Through the purity of all enlightened activities (*karmas*), such as pacifying and so forth, there is a variegated lotus. [Sentient beings...]

The seat of the solar mandala represents the purity of wisdom that utterly destroys the darkness of ignorance within the continuum of the body, dries up the mire of non-virtue, and brings the sprout of the bodhicitta to full maturity. The seat of the corpse represents the purity of having cleared away faults regarding reality, which is without entity and non-dual. Thus are the supports.

This is the purity of the support. Now, if one asks how the completion of the goddesses of the samayasattva should be performed, it is said: "The oral instructions of the guru," and so forth. The "oral instructions of the guru" are indeed the path; for by means of them, the siddhis follow after. "Stages" refers to meditation. "Extensive" means numerous. Furthermore, they are as follows: [they] abide upon the navel-lotus and the sun.

From the syllable *Bāṃ*, which is intensely blazing with red light rays, red light rays emanate like iron hooks. By means of the mudrā for summoning and drawing in the Wisdom Yoginīs and by reciting *Hem*, they are summoned and caused to enter into oneself.

In the *Lte ba la sogs par* (The Navel and Other Parts), one generates the syllables of the mantras beginning with *Oṃ Bāṃ*, and having empowered them with the three syllables, the Vajrayoginīs who have arrived together with the Wisdom Goddesses—holding skull-cups and *ḍamarus* filled with the nectar of wisdom—[chant] the verses beginning with: "Just as by the mere act of being born... and so forth.

While reciting [the mantra], slightly incline the skull cup held in the left hand so that a stream of the nectar of primordial wisdom (*jñānamṛta*) confers empowerment. Visualize yourself as being of the nature of great bliss (*mahāsukha*). From the excess water, visualize Vajrasattva or Vairocana perfectly complete upon the crown of your head. *Oṃ sarvata thāgata ābhiṣekatasamaya śrī*.

One should recite "YE HŪṂ HŪṂ PHAṬ. Then, one should offer worship with the offering goddesses and praise with the eight-line verse. One should cultivate the firm conviction that sentient beings, exhorted by rays of light, perform prostrations, offer praise, and make supplications. Then, having prepared the nectar according to the ritual procedure, [one visualizes] a vajra arising from a white HŪṂ.

With light rays from the tongue that have become one-pointed, resembling the hair of a jackal, or having mentally summoned them, one should intensely visualize oneself as the form of the Hero (Vīra) and the Sovereign Lady (Īśvarī), who are the embodiment of all the Tathāgatas free from attachment, and partake of the nectar. One should know that through this, sentient beings of the Sukhāvatī realm will abide in meditative absorption (samādhi).

Because it is not [otherwise], the seat and so forth must also be examined through the two truths of the reality of the maṇḍala. Following that, the meditation taught for the yogin who desires a firm mind to swiftly accomplish all siddhis is stated as: "Within her lotus," and so forth; this refers to the triangle (*cakra*) situated within the lotus of that Vajrayoginī.

Third, it shall be explained in detail that "one should meditate on the source of phenomena (dharmodaya). If one asks what that wheel is like: "All objects" refers to all worldly and transcendent desires. It is the "accomplisher of all objects" because it brings them to complete fulfillment. "The bestower of the accomplishment of all objects" means the state that brings all desired objects to completion without exception.

Regarding the phrase "How is it? Adorned with the three qualities at the sites of the marks," this means that the *lalanā*, *rasanā*, and *avadhūtī* channels are, by nature, *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. The meaning is that they are thoroughly adorned by those very natures. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "at the sites of the marks," this refers to the generation of all phenomena as the essence of Mahāmudrā.

Because it is the condition that serves as the basis for that [deity]. Furthermore, how is it? "Red in color" means it is even more intensely red than the *japā* flower. Therefore, "great light" means blazing and extremely radiant. Furthermore, how is the wheel? "The mantra’s syllables are complete" should be understood to mean that the syllable *Bāṃ* is situated in the center according to the oral instructions. *Vajra-yoginī*...

The meaning is that [the mantra] is completely filled within the center, which is itself completely filled by an upward-pointing garland of mantras. Furthermore, how is it? "Circulating" means with a swift movement, like the wheel of a potter. As for how the wheel is to be visualized, "rākṣasa" and so forth refers to a fierce rākṣasa.

The five aggregates, which are of the nature of fire, are like a demon because they are suitable to be consumed by the self that is non-apprehensible. His face is "effortful. His path is "drawn upward. Furthermore, what is it like? Regarding the phrase "Vairocana" and so forth: Vairocana-prabha is Caṇḍālī, because she is of the nature of fire. By her, Caṇḍālī, being intensely blazing—

Thus, the summarized meaning here is as follows: for the purpose of stabilizing the mind, the yogi should visualize the syllables Oṃ, Hūṃ, Āḥ, and Hāṃ at the knots located in the navel, heart, throat, and the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*). Then, the nature of Caṇḍālī, stirred by the wind and fire residing in the secret wheel, becomes the blazing syllable Āḥ.

One should visualize that the three syllables, such as *hāṃ*, together with the inseparable syllable *oṃ*—which has arisen simultaneously as the nature of joy—transform into a drop (*bindu*). Having cultivated this meditation and developed firm conviction through its full maturation, one should perceive that from that very *oṃ* alone, a single subtle ray of light blazes forth and remains. By the power of that, [the nectar...]

Because the *gong du* will begin to drip, the Lord (*Khyab bdag*) will arrive and that region will be cooled by his light rays; then, one should gaze at the *bindu* with one-pointed mind. One should recognize when stability has been attained through the signs. Once stability is attained, one should visualize that the various appearances of the light-ray rays become vividly clear.

One will see everything as clearly as if one were holding a *la-skyyu-ru* fruit in the palm of one's hand, and all meditative absorptions (*samādhi*) will also be swiftly perfected; this is the yoga of the drop (*binduyoga*). Following that, the supreme method for practicing the subtle yoga is taught: "From the sow’s face," and so forth, meaning that above a height of one cubit from the sow’s face, a swastika is completely [visualized].

Having looked at the surrounding circle, one should meditate on the wheel. Likewise, having placed the bodhicitta-bindu—the nature of innate joy (*sahajānanda*)—which has become of one taste with the syllables *haṃ* and so forth that have flowed out, and which is the size of a barley grain, upon the tip of the vajra-jewel or the lotus-anther for even a moment, one should focus one’s attention upon it. How...

When the verbal explanation has become firm, one sees the signs; then, one should emanate the maṇḍala of yoginīs such as Vajravārāhī—this is the subtle yoga (*sūkṣmayoga*). Some say that those whose mental continuums are afflicted by the conceptual afflictions should practice the meditation on the *yung drud*. Then, while the mind abides in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the wheel revolves at the secret place.

It is said, "BLTA'I. Furthermore, some, seeing [the breath] circling in a *śrīvatsa* (eternal knot), slightly restrain the face of the *rākṣasa*; from the blazing of the white light rays, they say, "Meditate on the wheel. That is to say: if the mind becomes stable in the *śrīvatsa*, the winds of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) will become stable. If the winds of exertion become stable, then through the fierce fire (*caṇḍālī*) moved by them, from the syllables such as *Haṃ*...

One should meditate on that secret wheel as well, which—through the descent of the nectar of faith—becomes a *bindu* whose nature is innate joy (*sahajānanda*). As it is said in the *Mahāsādhana*: "Following that, the wise one, within the element, in the interior of the three-peaked mountain, should meditate on a blazing red wheel revolving rapidly, as previously described, with the supreme power."

"Abiding as firm as [a mountain] made of *kyis*, and shining like a lamp unmoved in the absence of wind, one dwells in the mandala of great bliss (*mahāsukha*). Having performed the ritual purification by the dripping of the drops of nectar (*amṛta-bindu*), and so forth, up until the statement: 'One will attain Mahāmudrā'—this is the explanation. If one asks what is accomplished for a yogin who meditates in such a manner, it is called 'Mudrā'."

"La sog pa" (the one from La) refers to proceeding with joy, or because of the complete purity of emptiness through being free from all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). The two mudrās are the svastika and the wheel. In that regard, the ultimate application is non-dual gnosis (*advayajñāna*). Alternatively, it refers to the face of the rākṣasa being slightly contracted.

By means of the blazing of the two splendors of light (*rnam 'od dbyig gnyen rab tu 'bar ba*), there are the two mudrās. Alternatively, regarding the two—the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukha-cakra*) and the emanation wheel (*nirmāṇa-cakra*)—the application of the two mudrās is the union with the essence of great bliss. Through that, the accomplishment of the three realms as the three bodies (*trikāya*) is perfected. Furthermore, what need is there to mention minor accomplishments (*siddhi*) by means of the word "also"? [This includes] both the mundane and the supramundane.

This means that one will attain all the *phun sum tshogs pa* (perfections). If it is argued that one attains the *siddhis* by abiding in the generation stage (*utpattikrama*) alone, [the text replies] with the words "in an instant" and so forth; because there are no seeds, hand-symbols, and so on, "an instant" (*skad cig*) refers to simultaneity. "Aspect" (*rnam pa*) refers to the aspect of the deity. Its "yoga" (*rnal 'byor*) is the union of emptiness and compassion.

PA'O: "I" refers to myself, the yogin who possesses that very essence for a moment. Because the yogin possesses non-dual gnosis (*advayajñāna*), he will achieve accomplishment; that is to say, he will attain the siddhi of Mahāmudrā. "Not otherwise" means that there is no completion stage (*niṣpannakrama*). As it is said: "The two stages are the authentic support of the Vajra-holder."

The teaching of the Dharma was thus given. By means of the yogi who abides in the stages of generation (*utpattikrama*) and completion (*niṣpannakrama*), the siddhi of Mahāmudrā will be swiftly attained; this is the ritual procedure for meditation. The extraction of the mantras is easy to understand. Next, the explanation of the *bali* offering (*gtor ma*) is as follows: "Naked" (*gcer bu*) and so forth refers to one who is naked with loose hair, [staying] in the previously mentioned directions such as the west.

Regarding the statement, "Having visualized and blessed it according to the ritual manual, one should cast the *torma*," this shall be explained after the invocation. This refers to the following: upon a wind wheel generated from the syllable *yāṃ*, there is a fire mandala generated from the syllable *rāṃ*. Upon that, on three human heads arising from the syllable *kaṃ*, are the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and the five lamps within a lotus vessel arising from the syllable *āḥ*, together with the syllables *ha ho hrīḥ*.

Having discarded the ordinary color, smell, and potency of the [substances], visualize them as being melted by a fire fanned by the wind—like milk mixed with *sindhūra* after the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and so forth have been consumed—and then, by the syllable BAṂ arising from it, facing downward, they are churned and melted; beneath that, OṂ ĀḤ:

HŪṂ. By the light rays of the *bsgoms pa* (meditative visualization), the nectar from the ocean and other sources is summoned; this nectar is perfectly accomplished like the mercury of the siddhas. Through the three syllables, it is blessed according to one's desires. Having placed the assembly of Vajrayoginī and others—summoned by means of mantra and mudrā—in front, and having made pure offerings, [one visualizes] from a white HŪṂ a vajra...

To the Vajradākinī who possesses the marks of a son of the noble family, recite this mantra: *Oṃ vajra-dākini ai māṃ gṛhṇa gṛhṇa hūṃ phaṭ | oṃ jaḥ hūṃ baṃ hoḥ samaya-stvam dṛśya hoḥ*. For the dākinīs and so forth, [recite]: *oṃ vajra ā rali hoḥ jaḥ*.

"HŪṂ BĀṂ HOḤ, VAJRA DĒKINĪ SAMAYA STVAṂ DṚŚYA HOḤ. With these words, one should recite [the mantra] once, twice, three times, four times, or five times. Then, the offering to the guardians of the directions who dwell in the eight charnel grounds is as follows: OṂ KHA KHA KHĀHI KHĀHI, SARVA YAKṢARĀKṢASA, BHŪTA, PRETA, PIŚĀCA, ĀTMĀDA, KUMBHĀṆḌA, ĀPASMĀRA, DĀKINYA.

DA YA, AI MAm BA LIm, GRiHnA TU, SA MA YAm RKAsHA TU, MA MA SARBBA SIDDHI MME, PAR YTZATSAN TU, YA THEE BAm, YA THEshtAm, BHU NYDZA THA, PI PA THA, M'A TI KRA MA TH'A, MA MA SARBBA KARTA YA SATSU KHA, BI BRi DHA YE, SA HA YI KA BHA BANTU, H'Um H'Um PHAt PHAt SV'A H'A. Recite this seven times and present the offering. Having tasted the nectar, [experience] great bliss.

One should visualize the deities, beginning with the Vajrayoginī who is to be attained. Then, having been perfectly worshipped by the offering goddesses arisen from one's own seed-syllable (*bīja*), and praised with the eight-line mantra, one should supplicate for the attainment of the desired siddhi. Having abandoned faults such as excess or deficiency and requested forbearance, [one should perform the mudrā] with the ring finger and the thumb.

Taking the *se gol* (dice) in hand and reciting "Oṃ vajra muḥ," one should dissolve [the offering] into the seed-syllable of oneself as the master of the maṇḍala. This is the torma of the Bhagavatī. Regarding the term "samaya" (pledge): it is so called because one must not transgress it; thus, samaya refers to the vows regarding non-virtuous actions such as taking life and so forth. Furthermore, samaya is the joy arising from relying upon a wisdom consort (*prajñā*).

The sixteen drops (*bindu*) having become of one taste, their entry into the vajra-jewel is celibacy (*brahmacarya*). Furthermore, the commitment (*samaya*) is the nature of the ethical discipline (*śīla*) of those very sixteen drops of joy not being emitted. How so? From the vajra-jewel, they move upward to the secret place, the navel, the heart, the throat, and the *ūrṇā*-hair-tuft between the brows.

"Restraint is the secret samaya. As for eating, it is *go ku da ha na*: the food consisting of lamps and so forth, which has been transformed into nectar through the ritual procedures. If the samaya is impaired, various types of illnesses will arise, such as headaches and leprosy. Only by guarding the two samayas will siddhi be attained. Having prostrated to Vajravārāhī, on the [first] lunar day...

In the extensive ritual manual of the Ten Deities, for the benefit of practitioners, the Great Powerful One shall be proclaimed. The tenth day of the waxing moon is certain as it completely cuts through the net of the afflictions. Long ago, the Lion of the Śākyas attained enlightenment at the essence [of the site]; on the first day of the month, the Buddha Māyā became a Buddha on the tenth day of the waxing moon. What is the use of speaking much? All of those...

Emerging from the Tathāgata, Luipa, Virūpa, and the others attained the state of accomplished siddhas. Because of those very tenth days, they became possessors of incomparable merit. For them, there is meditative concentration, recitation, and likewise the fire offering (*homa*). To demonstrate the infinite fruit, at night, through the particularly sublime [practice], there is the wheel of heroes and yoginīs, the wheel of youth.

By means of the ritual stages of the siddhas, if one worships the Single One, one will attain the accomplishments (*siddhi*). Through the wind and mind that have gradually dissolved by means of the yogic play, the conceptual elaborations of the mind are greatly diminished; self-awareness is renowned as the "Full Moon" (*pūrṇimā*). Arising from the indestructible sound abiding through the guru’s oral instructions, the innate (*sahaja*) is explained as the "New Moon" (*amāvāsī*). The vital breath (*prāṇa*)...

On the tenth day of the waxing moon, by means of sporting upon the Middle Way, the inner heat (*caṇḍālī*) ascends; it strikes all the wheels at the crown of the head. This is the recollection of the tenth day of the body. Then, on the tenth day, having washed the *tila*, *kṣīraka* (milk-hemp), and barley grains, and while the practitioner remains in meditative equipoise, the various offerings will be accomplished. Following the stages of the *Guhyasamāja* and so forth, one should perform the worship of one’s respective *iṣṭadevatā*.

Especially at dusk, the practitioner should meditate upon that very reality. Having explained the realization through one’s own [experience], one should offer the *bali* as taught in the path of the Siddhas. The general sequence has been thoroughly explained; now the specific [details] shall be described. On the tenth day of the waxing moon, there are two offerings of *pūjā*; on the waning moon, there are two, consisting of *homa* and *pūjā*. On the tenth day of the final month of autumn, the heroic Siddhas of the path are empowered.

One who possesses a mind that is the nature of passion (*rāga*) should be honored with the finest wine; one should worship with red flowers beautifully entwined with *kunda* blossoms. The play of mental recitation is focused upon the subterranean realm (*pātāla*). With red sesame oil in a lamp, one should offer oblations (*homa*) using the essence of *nanti*. One should perform the fire sacrifice during the first watch of the night and dwell in meditation in a secluded place during the winter months. Or [one may wear] woolen cloth...

One should offer garments made of *rasabala* wool; one should worship with garlands of red flowers interspersed with well-strung yellow flowers. Reciting while playing hand-drums, one should perform the fire offering (*homa*) as described above during the waning moon, using black sesame on the ground above and below, followed by attendants. As before, one should employ the middling [offering] of red meat mixed with *kemikīra*, and worship as previously practiced. In the secret place...

The recitation with words and the play within the world of humans, which completely destroys all outflows—likewise, the fire offering (*homa*) to Yīlaka should be correctly performed at midnight. On the tenth day of the waning moon of the last month of winter, one should offer fragrant butter mixed with golden sprouts and flowers; the worship should be performed as before. The mental recitation and play are for the station of the brow.

On the tenth day of the waxing moon of the month when the [constellation] has shifted, one should perform a fire offering (*homa*) of *ariṅku*; this is the recollection for the first watch. During the waxing moon of the first month of winter, one should offer molasses and ginger mixed with *pāṭala* flowers; one should worship with red flowers. Through recitation, together with the flavor of the fierce play (*līlā*) established in Akaniṣṭha, one should perform the fire offering during the morning watch with the seed-syllable of the cave (*phuṅ sa bon*) in the waxing moon.

In the middle month of spring as well, on the tenth day, one should likewise perform worship with red *aśoka* flowers. With verbal recitation and play, one should offer stainless goat’s curd along with sugar. One should perform a fire offering (*homa*) of sesame oil, *sumana* flowers, and honey mixed with butter. During the waxing moon of the last month of spring, [one should offer] *karavīra*...

The physical offering, the mental recitation, and the playful union—these are the supreme means of shaking Mount Meru. Having fully wrapped [the body] with the arms crossed, one should offer fine garments of silk. One should perform the burnt offering (*homa*) with pills mixed with sesame oil. During the first half of the month of Āṣāḍha (the first summer month), one should offer lamps, medicinal wind-remedies, and sesame oil. One should worship with sprouts and flowers beautifully entwined with red blossoms.

Regarding the playful recitation for the purpose of slaying: "The path of emptiness is that which causes one to see; with ghee and oil as the fuel, one should constantly perform the fire offering (*homa*). During the middle month of summer, in the waxing phase of the moon, one should offer a *karavīra* flower. The verbal recitation and the playful [performance] should be observed by one's own hand. One should present a bowl filled with honey, or else a sword. This is the accomplishment of the dark fortnight.

Accompanied by the *pāyasa* [milk-rice] offering, one should perform the fire sacrifice (*homa*). During the summer months, one should worship with *jāba*, *bandhūka*, and *yandisa*. As for the yogic recitation and play, it is clearly observed at the root of the nose. One should offer a cloth smeared with white *guggulu* or *phra tsil*. The fire sacrifice should be performed with ghee and rice; likewise, with sesame oil mixed with white butter. This continues until the first month of autumn.

One should worship with *kahlāra*, *nāgakeśara*, water-born flowers, *utpala*, and *kumuda*. One’s own playful recitation of the mantra should be focused like gazing at the stars in the sky. On the tenth day of the waxing moon of the middle autumn month, one should offer *juna*, *jugala*, *lham-zho-chu*, and well-known fragrant substances; it is renowned that this fire offering (*homa*) with butter and *d’ur-ba* grass benefits all beings. One should worship with red *aindīvara*. [Fragrant]...

With the flowers of the *Mdog bzang*, one should please the *iṣṭadevatā*. The recitation of words arises in the secret place; together with the *rasanā* and *lalanā*, the mudrā that destroys Mount Meru should be known as the universally renowned. The yogin’s garment, the yogin’s staff, and the very method for meditating on yoga—these should be offered by the master who abides in perfect samādhi, as previously explained regarding the form. *Mar dor*.

For fragrant substances, one should burn ghee together with *ākāru*. Sesame seeds and accomplished substances—combine all these with all purifying agents. *Palāśa*, *arka*, *kaśmīra*, *patra*, *audumbara*, *khadira*, *palāśa*, *aśvattha*, *kapittha*, *durvā*, and *śana*: these sacrificial woods (*yājñika-kāṣṭha*) are to be burned in succession starting from the last month of autumn (*kārttika*). Or else, as follows:

Having obtained [the materials] according to the ritual manual, one should offer everything together with the substances for accomplishment. Desiring accomplishments that are pleasing to the mind, a man or a woman should offer them in a vessel of bronze mixed with *vīra-cūrṇa*. To achieve yogic accomplishments and to subdue Māras, one should present the sacrificial cake (*bali*). For the sake of desiring a son, one should joyfully offer wine as honey.

"Wherever one desires excellence, whatever that excellence may be, for those who desire inexhaustible results, one should offer [the feast] on the tenth day. Therein, the secret gift is the supreme among all gifts; whatever forms of joy arise from the mental conceptualizations of the practitioner, those become the seeds of accomplishment."

Therefore, the secret gift is the supreme means for accomplishing all aims. For the yogin who has not yet reached full maturation, regarding the siddhi of experiencing the monthly menses: it is the woman who exhausts sin, and she who causes the qualities of the Buddha to increase. To whomever one may have a desire, to them one should give in that manner. In whatever birth one gave [this gift] when the monthly menses occurred, [the merit of] the past—

In his tenth birth, that Lord became a Buddha; in his ninth birth, he was Lūipa; from his [eighth] ninth birth, Virūpa arose. In his fifth birth, he was Śavaripa; in his sixth birth, he was Dārika. What need is there for many? All these have attained the state of the Siddhas. On the tenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Caitra, the one who was most capable in giving—his account is found in the *Siddhāntamālā* of the Siddhas.

It is described in detail: when the sound of a crow is heard, on the tenth day, one should place the ten syllables of Tārā in the mudrā of Kākī. By reciting the mantra through meditative concentration (*samādhi*), even if death or an obstacle has occurred, there is no doubt that one will be victorious. At that very time, while reciting the three-syllable mantra, if one offers water from the hollow of one's palms a hundred times, within one year—

When Vajravārāhī draws in the ḍākinīs who are desired and pleasing to the mind, what need is there for much talk? At that time, everything will be accomplished. Through the ritual of the branch of siddhi, Vajravārāhī, together with the difficult rites, one will obtain the supreme siddhi by means of the homa offering of sesame seeds at the auspicious times. This is the section on the homa offerings of the ḍākinīs of the accomplished siddhas and siddhās.

By performing burnt offerings (*homa*) on the tenth day, even those who agitate people will attain accomplishments (*siddhi*). Through meditative concentration, generosity, and burnt offerings, as well as through worship, one brings satisfaction to the maṇḍala. Furthermore, the fruit that arises from [generosity] on the tenth day becomes ten thousandfold. Offerings of saffron, sindūra, kausumbha, fine garments, and menstrual blood are especially sublime when given on the tenth day.

In an open space where there is no roof-covering, the wise should offer a *bali* to the crows. When the sun has set, one should give a *bali* to the *kukura*. To those that appear as the sun sets, one should offer a *bali* for the sake of joy. Having offered the *bali* at night, one should cause the assembly of *śrāvakas* to rejoice. By means of this special *bali* on the tenth day, great accomplishments (*siddhi*) will arise.

From the *Twenty-Four Thousand [Verse]*, having extracted the essential meaning: this is the ritual for the tenth day, which should be performed by compassionate scholars. It must not be given to disciples who are unsubdued, even if they are masters of wealth. It should be bestowed upon those with disciplined faculties who abide in the lineage of the accomplished ones (*siddhas*). Otherwise, the lineage of the accomplished ones, as well as the vessel and awakening, will decline.

In particular, regarding the ocean of siddhis, the ritual for the fire offering (*homa*) has been explained by me in detail according to that source text; therefore, let the wise take it into their experience. By whatever merit I have gained through this work composed out of a desire to benefit sentient beings, may the multitudes of sentient beings be forever free from the afflictions. This concludes the commentary on the Glorious Vajrayoginī, the *Daśamīpūjā* (The Offering of the Tenth Day).
This concludes the work composed by the great mahāsiddha Dārikapa.

It was translated from the divine language into the Tibetan language, without error, by the great and glorious scholar Dānaśīla, a paṇḍita from Jagattalā in Eastern India, at the Ṛṣi-Ṣṛṅga mountain (Drang srong Srin po ri) in Central Tibet; it is thus self-manifested. This concludes [the translation].

The mantra for the torma of the crow and so forth is written as follows: Oṃ klām klām klām dharmatā āḥ kla śvātiriṇaḥ siddhi vayasanaḥ kāmbaya śāmpala siddha kākasaṃtana prasuta kāka balim gṛhṇata klām klām klām svāhā. Oṃ shlām shlām shlām ā pratistha tsalā tsirīṇaḥ.

The Essence Composed by Śrīḍākaravajra, together with the mudrās for bestowing food and the mudrā for averting misfortune, and the Mahāmudrā; [this is] the teaching on the summary of the meaning of the essence through the yoga of the Paṇḍita Nāgadatta. It was translated from the language of the gods into the Tibetan language as a self-translation by the great Paṇḍita of Eastern India, Dānaśīla, at the hermitage of the Siddha Ṛṣi Rākṣasaparvata.
